title: Decomposition: Divide and Conquer
objective: After this lesson you will be able to split compound tasks into staged prompts (extract → decide → draft), chain them with explicit handoffs, and add checklist verification that catches skipped steps.
why: 'Read this ticket, decide the policy, check history, draft the reply, and log it' fails as one prompt the way a five-table join without aliases fails — too many jobs, one breath. Decomposition gives each step its own instruction, its own output contract, and its own verifiable handoff. Reliability comes from staging, and staging is a design skill, not a model upgrade.

blocks.text: Split by verb, not by hope

Decompose along **verbs**: extract (pull facts), decide (classify/policy), draft (write), verify (check). Each stage gets the full four-part treatment (Ch.1) at small scope — and small scopes follow instructions dramatically better than compound ones. The split test: if you can't name each stage's output contract, you haven't split, you've just reworded.

blocks.code:
MONOLITH: Read the ticket, check policy + history, decide, reply, log. (5 jobs, 1 breath)

STAGED:
  S1 extract: ticket -> {order_id, issue, dates} (JSON, Ch.3 contract)
  S2 decide:  facts + policy text -> {approved, reason} (JSON)
  S3 draft:   decision + tone rules -> reply text (<=60 words)
  S4 verify:  reply + checklist -> {pass, fixes[]} (JSON)
Each stage independently testable, re-runnable, and replaceable.
blocks.caption: Verbs become stages; stages get contracts; contracts enable checks

blocks.text: Stages connect through **handoffs**: S1's JSON feeds S2's input slot, nothing else. Handoffs must be typed (the contract from Ch.3), logged (each stage's in/out persisted for debugging), and minimal (pass facts, not raw tickets — narrowed context per stage also saves budget, Ch.8). A stage that needs the original ticket alongside S1's output signals a bad split — re-cut until handoffs suffice.

blocks.caption: Handoffs typed, logged, minimal — stages as replaceable units

blocks.text: The verify stage runs a **checklist** against the draft: approved-decision stated? remedy exactly one? ≤60 words? no promised timelines? forbidden phrases absent? Checklists convert 'be careful' (ignored) into testable assertions (enforced) — and failed checks route back to re-draft with the specific fix, not a vague 'try again'.

blocks.caption: Verify mechanics deterministically; reserve the model for judgment

blocks.title: Run the checklist
blocks.note: Run it: expect {pass:true} then {pass:false} with two fixes (length + unapproved promise). Mechanics verify in code — fast, free, deterministic — while tone and correctness stay model-judged.

items: Split by verbs (extract/decide/draft/verify), each with its own output contract
Handoffs typed, logged, minimal — a stage needing raw inputs signals a bad split
Verify with checklists: mechanics in deterministic code, judgment to the model; failures route back with specific fixes

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice verifier on a reply of your design that fails exactly one check; report which. (b) Split 'triage + respond + log a billing dispute' into three stages with per-stage output contracts. (c) State which checks go in code vs model judgment, with one example each.
hints: Craft a reply failing exactly one check: e.g. 61+ words but otherwise clean (length), or promise-free but missing 'label' (offer). Report the single fix.
Stages: extract (amounts/dates → JSON) → decide (policy → {adjust, reason}) → draft+verify (reply + checklist). Contracts per stage, handoffs named.
Code: length, forbidden phrases, required offer keywords. Model: tone appropriateness, reason correctness, policy interpretation.
exercise.why: Decomposition is designed twice: once in stages, once in verification assignment. Code-vs-model split by check type is the reliability insight — determinism where possible, judgment where necessary.
exercise.code: // Single-failure probe pattern (playground): craft, run, report the one fix.

quiz.q: Five-job monolith prompt underperforms. First move?
options: Split by verbs into staged prompts with per-stage output contracts and typed handoffs
quiz.explain: Compound scope defeats instruction-following before model quality matters. Staging gives each job its own contract, handoff, and testability.

quiz.q: Stage 2 needs the raw ticket plus Stage 1's output. Meaning?
options: Bad split: handoffs should suffice; re-cut until each stage needs only its inputs
quiz.explain: Handoff insufficiency diagnoses decomposition failure. Well-cut stages consume typed handoffs only — raw-input hunger means the boundary is wrong.

options: In deterministic code — mechanics verify free and exactly; reserve the model for tone/correctness judgment
quiz.explain: Deterministic where possible (mechanics), model where necessary (judgment). Code checks run fast, free, and identically every time.

summary: Verbs become stages, stages get contracts, handoffs stay typed/logged/minimal, checklists verify (code for mechanics, model for judgment). Reliability is staged, not wished.
next: Staged work behaves — now bound it: scope limits, injection defense, and refusals with grace. Next: guardrails.
